chapter_title: Concerning the Dragon with Fourteen Heads; what it is and [...]
chapter_note: The chapter’s teaching substrate is a systematic microcosm mapping: the “dragon” is a spiritual force/thought associated with the body, having fourteen “heads” (sense/torso faculties) and five “dens” (internal organs). This is largely CORE in ¶3–¶6, with Q&A framing in ¶1–¶2 and a closing disciple-response in ¶9. ¶7–¶8 show late drift toward exhortation and Manichaean institutional labels (“elect”), consistent with the strong chapter-level editorial fatigue signal.

paragraphs.core_text: They say that there is a dragon with fourteen heads, and it is gathered in and [ ... ] den with five refuges. What really is a corporeal dragon with fourteen heads? Or is it another spiritual lesson?
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed hagiographic/dialogue frame and address: "[Once again], one of his disciples asked the apostle ... Now, I beseech you, my master, that you may instruct me ..."
paragraphs.temporal_note: Q&A container and honorific address (“disciple… apostle… my master… beseech”) indicate FRAME, but the question itself is structurally specific (14 heads, 5 refuges) and likely preserves the topic-heading of an older teaching unit.

paragraphs.core_text: There is never a dragon in the flesh with fourteen heads, as the Magi say! Rather, this is a spiritual lesson. It was uttered in virginity [ ... ] the Magi did not understand [ ... ] all their words that are written [ ... spiri]tual (?).
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue attribution: "Then the apostle says to him:"
paragraphs.temporal_note: Dialogue attribution is a later compilation frame marker (“apostle says…”). The remaining content is definitional/clarificatory (spiritual vs. fleshly) and functions as the opening thesis of the teaching.

paragraphs.core_text: Again, this is how this earth [ ... ] to it, as it is accounted a corporeal dragon [ ... ] I will instruct you [ ... ] the Dragon is this doctrine [ ... ] of the flesh [ ... ] also the fourteen heads that are distributed over the Dragon are these.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal explanatory voice moving into a numbered/partitioned exposition (“the fourteen heads… are these”) matches the correspondential substrate. “Dragon” is capitalized here as a personified operative force.

paragraphs.core_text: The seven sense organs on the head of the body are the two of sight by which one sees; the two of sound by which one hears; the two of scent by which one smells; also the tongue [ ... ] by which one selects, receiving there the different tastes that occur in every form.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure microcosm structure: enumerated faculties/organs mapped as the “heads,” with sensory correspondences (sight/sound/scent/taste). No institutional or exhortative reach beyond the system.

paragraphs.core_text: These are the seven heads of the dragon, the seven sense organs that are on the upper part of the person; [ ... ] below. The seven of the torso are these: two [ ... ]; the two [ ... ] ruler [ ... ] the seven heads that are above; so with the ones below they total and make fourteen heads of the dragon.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Continuation of the systematic partition (upper vs. below; totals to fourteen). This is classic substrate list-building: structure completes itself without application to church life.

paragraphs.core_text: Conversely, the five dens about which they have spoken, where the Dragon is congregated and protrudes, are these: the first is the tongue; the second is the lungs; the third is the heart; the fourth is the spleen; the fifth is the blood that dwells in them. Again, if it shall look out from them [and reveal its likeness and its observation above and below, it wages war by] its fourteen heads.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Highly systematic “five dens” enumeration mapped to internal organs, plus internal mechanics (“look out… wages war”)—still cosmos/body-system→system, not cosmos→institution. Capitalized “Dragon” as an agent.

paragraphs.core_text: Whoever will recognise them with the dragon, which is the thought of the body, and struggles with it and is victorious and kills it in them He receives the victory without suffering on the day of his coming forth.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed institutional naming formula and identity labels: "[ ... he is called] the holy righteous one, elect, good person."
paragraphs.temporal_note: This paragraph pivots from description to application: second-person/virtue framing (“whoever… struggles… victorious”) and especially the institutional term “elect” mark a later pastoralizing use of the teaching. The definitional clause (“the dragon… is the thought of the body”) reads as older substrate.

paragraphs.core_text: the dragon that exists with its fourteen heads and five dens, wherein it is concealed and hidden. It does through them [ ... / its des]ire all the time.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed didactic closure/address: "So, behold, I have taught you of"
paragraphs.temporal_note: Summative restatement of the internal mechanism (concealed in dens; operates through desire) looks like substrate recap, but the “I have taught you… behold” closure is typical of compiled catechetical delivery and likely secondary.
Disciple’s reaction speech with blessing/praise (“My heart has been persuaded… Blessed is every one…”) is a classic hagiographic/edifying frame closure rather than system-description.
